sections.label: Content note
sections.body: **Content note:** this page discusses the abuse of children in foster care, restraint, the drugging of children, and the deaths of children. [Where to report abuse is listed below.](#kop-ri-report)

sections.label: Not the troubled teen industry
sections.heading: Not the troubled teen industry
sections.body:
Foster care is not part of the troubled teen industry, and Kids Over Profits does not track foster homes, foster care agencies or state child welfare systems. We do track the therapeutic group homes and residential treatment centers where states place children from foster care; they are in our [directory](/tti-program-index/).

The two systems hold the same children. A child in foster care is in the custody of a state, county or tribal agency, and the agency, not a parent, decides where the child lives. Agencies send these children, many with no need for treatment, to the same residential treatment centers parents pay for, often in another state, where they are restrained, drugged and abused by companies paid by the child and by the day. Several companies run both foster care and youth residential programs.

We are not experts on foster care. The people who grew up in it, and the organizations listed below, are.

sections.label: What foster care is
sections.heading: What foster care is
sections.body:
On September 30, 2024, 328,947 children were in foster care in the United States, and 505,682 spent time in it during the year. 39 percent lived with relatives and 28 percent in non-relative foster homes. 28,365 were in therapeutic foster homes, and about 35,000 in group homes, institutions or residential care.[^1] Residential placements have fallen, from about 101,000 children (19 percent) in 2002 to about 34,000 (9 percent) in 2022.[^2]

Child welfare agencies spent $34.3 billion in 2022,[^3] $9.5 billion of it from Title IV-E of the Social Security Act, the main federal foster care program.[^4] Medicaid pays residential treatment a daily rate for each child.[^5]

States keep custody but contract the work out. In a 2015 Senate Finance Committee survey, 31 of the 33 states that answered used private agencies, and 16 contracted with for-profit as well as nonprofit providers.[^6] Private agencies recruit and supervise foster homes and run therapeutic foster care, group homes, shelters and residential treatment.

The Family First Prevention Services Act of 2018 stops Title IV-E payments for a child in a group setting after 14 days unless the setting meets set requirements, as a Qualified Residential Treatment Program (QRTP) does.[^7] QRTPs are not bound by the restraint and seclusion rules that psychiatric residential treatment facilities must follow.[^5]

sections.label: History
sections.heading: Where foster care came from
sections.body:
Foster care and the troubled teen industry grew from the same institutions: the houses of refuge and orphanages that took poor children from their families.

The New York House of Refuge (1825) held children taken from "corrupting environments," mostly immigrant neighborhoods, for indefinite terms of labor, corporal punishment and religious instruction, and let them go when they were judged obedient. In *Ex parte Crouse* (1838) the Pennsylvania Supreme Court upheld the state's power to confine a child without due process ([disability timeline](/idd-timeline/)). The Philadelphia House of Refuge became Glen Mills Schools, which [closed in 2019](/juvenile-justice-timeline/) after widespread abuse allegations.

From 1854 to 1929 the orphan trains sent children west to families who often used them as labor. Many were not orphans: in one charity's figures for 1857 to 1858, 65 percent had at least one living parent ([orphan care timeline](/orphanages/)).[^8]

Foster care began to replace orphanages after the 1909 White House Conference on Dependent Children declared a home better than an institution. As orphanages emptied between the 1960s and 1980s, poor children moved into psychiatric and behavioral facilities ([orphan care timeline](/orphanages/)). Boys Town, an orphanage in 1917, runs residential treatment today. In July 1991 Straight, Inc.'s Boston branch closed when Massachusetts pulled its foster care license. Private equity firms have owned The MENTOR Network, now Sevita, since 2001, and Sequel Youth & Family Services passed from one private equity owner to the next from 2010 ([corporatization timeline](/corporatization/)).

sections.label: How it is connected to the TTI
sections.heading: How it is connected to the troubled teen industry
sections.body:
### The same facilities

State agencies send children in foster care to the residential treatment centers parents pay for, often when they need nothing a facility offers. The Senate Finance Committee's 2024 investigation of Universal Health Services, Acadia Healthcare, Devereux Advanced Behavioral Health and Vivant Behavioral Healthcare found that "a significant portion of foster children placed at RTFs have no demonstrated behavioral health needs." In 2013, 28.8 percent of children in congregate care had "No Clinical Indicators."[^5] ([Our summary of the report](/warehouses-of-neglect/).)

All four companies are in our records: [Universal Health Services](/operator/universal-health-services/) with more than 70 programs, [Devereux](/operator/devereux-advanced-behavioral-health/) with 43, [Acadia Healthcare](/operator/acadia-healthcare/) with 13 and [Vivant Behavioral Health](/operator/vivant-behavioral-health/) with 5. So is [Sequel](/operator/sequel-tsi/), with 42 programs, most now closed, which took in children from more than 40 states and territories.[^9]

### What happens to them there

In 2020 staff at Lakeside Academy, a Sequel facility in Michigan, restrained Cornelius Fredericks, 16, a child in foster care, on the floor for about 12 minutes. He died, and the medical examiner ruled his death a homicide.[^10] At Universal Health Services' Provo Canyon School in Utah, a 14-year-old Oregon foster child with an intellectual disability was physically restrained and chemically sedated more than 30 times in four months.[^5] Illinois sent foster children to Acadia-run facilities in Arkansas, Indiana and Michigan where police logs recorded assaults and reports of sexual abuse.[^11]

### Sent out of state

In fiscal year 2021 nearly 2,400 children in foster care were placed in residential facilities in another state.[^7] The interstate compact that governs foster placements across state lines does not cover residential treatment centers or group homes. Oregon brought every one of its out-of-state foster children home in June 2020 and ended its contract with Sequel, which held most of them.[^12] The GAO asked HHS in 2022 to help states share what works in preventing maltreatment in residential facilities; HHS agreed, and by June 2024 had not acted.[^2]

States give a shortage of placements as the reason they send children away. At home, children wait: Kentucky's ombudsman reviewed 49 children who slept in state office buildings between June and October 2024. One stayed 35 days, and the youngest was a year old.[^13]

### The same people

Jay Ripley co-founded Sequel in 1999, after co-founding the juvenile justice contractor Youth Services International, later owned and run by James F. Slattery ([juvenile justice timeline](/juvenile-justice-timeline/)). In 2015 Ripley told an interviewer that Sequel sought children whose placements the government pays for, and that "you can make money in this business if you control staffing." In 2021 he founded Vivant, which bought 13 of Sequel's facilities. Three senior Vivant leaders came from Sequel, among them its former vice president of operations, who joined a month after leaving.[^5]

### Companies that run both

- **Devereux** recruits foster parents[^14] and runs residential programs for children in several states.
- **KidsPeace** runs foster care, residential campuses in Pennsylvania, Georgia and Maine, and a psychiatric hospital in Pennsylvania.[^15] Four of its programs are in our records.
- **Boys Town** runs foster care[^16] and residential programs, several of them in our records.
- **Youth Villages** runs foster care[^17] and five residential campuses in Tennessee and Georgia,[^18] which are in our records.

sections.label: What investigations have found
sections.heading: What investigations have found
sections.body:
- **No one can count the abuse (HHS Inspector General, 2024).** 16 states lacked the information to spot patterns of maltreatment in residential facilities, and 32 did not formally track whether a facility's owner ran facilities in other states. 13 did not consistently report whether a maltreated child lived in a residential facility, so the Inspector General could not count abuse in these facilities nationwide.[^7]
- **Harm built into the business (Senate Finance Committee, 2024).** *Warehouses of Neglect* found that providers fill facilities to capacity while cutting staff to widen their margin on each day's rate, and that the abuse by staff and overuse of restraint and seclusion that follow are "endemic to the RTF operating model."[^5]
- **Little value to the children (Think of Us, 2021).** 78 young people who had lived in group homes, shelters and residential treatment while in foster care described their placements in *Away From Home*. Most "found little to no long term value from them."[^19]
- **Sequel (APM Reports, 2020).** Reporters compiled more than 8,600 emergency calls from Sequel facilities in 18 states, and found 20 cases since 2010 in which government investigators found staff in sexual or romantic relationships with residents.[^9]
- **Devereux (2020).** After the Philadelphia Inquirer reported a 25-year pattern of sexual abuse by staff, Philadelphia's child welfare and behavioral health agencies moved to remove 53 children from Devereux facilities.[^20]
- **Psychotropic drugs (GAO, 2011; HHS Inspector General, 2018).** Foster children in five states were prescribed psychotropic drugs at higher rates than other children on Medicaid; hundreds took five or more at once, and some were infants.[^21] Seven years later, one in three foster children on these drugs in five states did not get the treatment planning or monitoring their states required.[^22]
- **A for-profit foster care company (Senate Finance Committee, 2017).** The MENTOR Network, then majority owned by the private equity firm Vestar Capital Partners, served 10,300 foster children in 18 states. Maryland found violations in 20 of 22 quarterly reviews, and MENTOR kept operating there. Most children who died in its care were never the subject of an internal investigation.[^6] Its foster care now runs under the name Sevita.[^23]

sections.label: Where to report abuse
sections.heading: Where to report abuse
sections.body:
- **If a child is in danger right now**, call [911](tel:911).
- **State child protective services (CPS):** every state takes reports of child abuse and neglect, including abuse in foster homes, group homes and residential facilities. Find yours in the federal [list of state reporting numbers](https://www.childwelfare.gov/state-child-abuse-and-neglect-reporting-numbers/). Abuse in a facility is investigated by the state where the facility is, so report a child placed out of state there, and tell the child's caseworker and the agency that placed the child.
- **Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline**, call or text, 24 hours, in more than 170 languages: 1-800-422-4453. Childhelp does not take reports itself; its counselors help you reach the right agency.
- **Protection and Advocacy agencies:** every state has a federally mandated legal advocacy agency for people with disabilities, including children harmed in residential treatment centers and hospitals. [Find your state's agency](https://www.ndrn.org/about/ndrn-member-agencies/).
- **988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline**, 24 hours: call or text [988](tel:988).

Our [reporting directory](/report-abuse/) lists each state's agencies, hotlines and licensing offices.

sections.label: Organizations to learn from
sections.heading: Learn from the people who work on this
sections.body:
- [FosterClub](https://www.fosterclub.com/): A national network for young people in and from foster care, "built for youth, powered by youth," whose Lived Experience Leaders speak to lawmakers and agencies.
- [Foster Youth in Action](https://www.fosteryouthaction.org/): Founded in 2008 by foster youth organizers. A national network of youth-led groups working to change the foster care system.
- [Think of Us](https://www.thinkofus.org/): A foster care research and policy organization led and guided by people with lived experience. Publisher of *Away From Home*, on institutional placements.
- [Children's Rights](https://www.childrensrights.org/): Brings legal action against state systems, including to stop the unnecessary institutionalization of children.
- [National Center for Youth Law](https://youthlaw.org/): Impact litigation and policy work on foster care, youth justice, health and education.
- [Juvenile Law Center](https://jlc.org/): Advocates for the rights of young people in the child welfare and justice systems.
- [The Imprint](https://imprintnews.org/): An independent nonprofit daily newsroom covering child welfare and youth justice, including its "Medicated in Foster Care" series.

sections.label: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.heading: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.body: If you grew up in foster care, work in it, or know something on this page is wrong or out of date, please [tell us](/contact/). We will correct it.
